questions.title: Why does preserving hyperspherical energy guarantee semantic preservation in diffusion model fine‑tuning?
questions.question_body:
The paper claims that keeping the hyperspherical energy of a layer unchanged during fine‑tuning preserves the model’s generative semantics. I understand that hyperspherical energy is defined as 
\[\text{HE}(\mathbf{W}) = \sum_{i\neq j} \|\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i-\hat{\mathbf{w}}_j\|^{-1}\]\nwith \(\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i=\mathbf{w}_i/\|\mathbf{w}_i\|\). How does the pair‑wise angle similarity between neurons directly relate to the ability of the diffusion model to generate diverse, high‑fidelity images? Could someone explain the intuition and any empirical evidence that supports this hypothesis?

questions.title: How does an orthogonal transformation in OFT avoid destroying pre‑training knowledge?
questions.question_body: Equation (5) states that applying an orthogonal matrix \(\mathbf{R}\) to the pretrained weight matrix \(\mathbf{W}^0\) preserves the hyperspherical energy because \(\mathbf{R}\hat{\mathbf{w}}_i = \widehat{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{w}}_i\). Intuitively, I see that rotations preserve dot‑products, but why is that sufficient to guarantee that the model’s pre‑trained representation power is retained? Is there a formal argument that shows the distance between the transformed weights and the original weights is solely due to rotation, and why this does not impact the diffusion process?

questions.title: Can you explain the difference between COFT’s angular deviation constraint and the usual small‑learning‑rate fine‑tuning?
questions.question_body: The Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT) adds the constraint \(\|\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{I}\|\le\epsilon\) to limit how far the orthogonal matrix can deviate from the identity. The paper mentions this provides stability similar to a small learning rate. How is this constraint different from simply training with a very small learning rate? Does it impose a stricter bound on the norm of the weight update, and how does that translate to the actual changes in neuron directions?

questions.title: What role does the Cayley transform play in maintaining orthogonality during training?
questions.question_body: To enforce the orthogonality constraint efficiently, the authors use the Cayley parameterization \(\mathbf{R}=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) with \(\mathbf{Q}\) skew‑symmetric. How does this representation guarantee that \(\mathbf{R}\) remains orthogonal at every training step? Are there numerical issues with the matrix inverse, especially for large dimensionality, and how does the block‑diagonal approximation help mitigate these?

questions.title: Why does orthogonal fine‑tuning converge faster than LoRA or standard fine‑tuning?
questions.question_body: The experiments report that OFT and COFT converge more quickly than LoRA and standard fine‑tuning methods. Is there a theoretical explanation for why restricting updates to the unit hypersphere leads to a smoother optimization landscape? Does this relate to the geometry of gradient descent on manifolds or to the fact that neuron directions are more semantically meaningful than their magnitudes?

questions.title: How does the re‑scaled OFT variant (adding a diagonal scaling matrix) affect hyperspherical energy?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces a re‑scaled OFT where the forward pass becomes \(\mathbf{z}=(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\mathbf{D})^{\top}\mathbf{x}\) with \(\mathbf{D}=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,\dots,s_n)\). Since scaling changes magnitudes but not directions, does the hyperspherical energy truly remain unchanged? If so, how does adding \(\mathbf{D}\) increase the expressiveness of the fine‑tuning without breaking the core OFT principle?

questions.title: Can orthogonal matrices from multiple fine‑tune tasks be composed without loss of knowledge?
questions.question_body: In the conclusions, the authors speculate that orthogonal matrices learned from different downstream tasks could be multiplied together, retaining orthogonality. Would composing several such matrices (e.g., \(\mathbf{R}_1\mathbf{R}_2\)) preserve the trained semantics from both tasks? What theoretical or empirical evidence is there that the resulting model still performs well on each individual task, and could there be interference effects?

questions.title: How does the block‑diagonal parameterization bias the learned orthogonal matrices?
questions.question_body: The block‑diagonal structure of \(\mathbf{R}\) is introduced to reduce parameter count, but it presumably limits the space of allowable rotations. In practice, how much flexibility is lost compared to a full orthogonal matrix? Are there examples where this bias leads to sub‑optimal results, and could alternative sparsity patterns or low‑rank approximations offer a better trade‑off?

questions.title: Why minimize hyperspherical energy is unsuitable for image generation but useful for classification?
questions.question_body: The authors contrast their approach with Liu et al.’s work on training classifiers, which seeks to minimize hyperspherical energy. I’m unclear why a lower energy (more uniform distribution of neurons on the sphere) would harm a generative diffusion model. Can someone explain why uniformity is beneficial for classification but detrimental for preserving the broad generative capabilities of a diffusion net?

questions.title: How is the control consistency metric defined and why is it reliable for evaluating controllable generation?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces a new control consistency metric that compares the control signal extracted from the generated image to the original input control signal. For example, for the Canny‑to‑image task they compute IoU and F1. Could a reader explain the exact pipeline: which off‑the‑shelf detector or segmentation model is used, how the loss is computed, and why this metric is a better indicator of controllability than standard qualitative inspection?
